In [[mathematics]], a '''dissipative operator''' is a [[linear operator]] ''A'' defined on a [[linear subspace]] ''D''(''A'') of [[Banach space]] ''X'', taking values in ''X'' such that for all ''λ'' > 0 and all ''x'' ∈ ''D''(''A'')

:<math>\|(\lambda I-A)x\|\geq\lambda\|x\|.</math>

A couple of equivalent definitions are given below. A dissipative operator is called '''maximally dissipative''' if it is dissipative and for all ''λ'' > 0 the operator ''λI'' − ''A'' is surjective, meaning that the range when applied to the domain ''D'' is the whole of the space ''X''.

An operator that obeys a similar condition but with a plus sign instead of a minus sign (that is, the negation of a dissipative operator) is called an '''accretive operator'''.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia|title=Dissipative operator|url=http://www.encyclopediaofmath.org/index.php/Dissipative_operator|encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Mathematics]]}}</ref>

The main importance of dissipative operators is their appearance in the [[Lumer–Phillips theorem]] which characterizes maximally dissipative operators as the generators of [[contraction semigroup]]s.

==Properties==
A dissipative operator has the following properties:<ref>Engel and Nagel Proposition II.3.14</ref>
* From the inequality given above, we see that for any ''x'' in the domain of ''A'', if ‖''x''‖ ≠ 0 then <math>\|(\lambda I-A)x\|\ne 0,</math> so the [[kernel (algebra)|kernel]] of ''λI'' − ''A'' is just the [[zero vector]] and ''λI'' − ''A'' is therefore [[injective]] and has an inverse for all ''λ'' > 0. (If we have the [[strict inequality]] <math>\|(\lambda I-A)x\|>\lambda\|x\|</math> for all non-null ''x'' in the domain, then, by the [[triangle inequality]], <math>\|\lambda x\|+\|Ax\|\ge\|(\lambda I-A)x\|>\lambda\|x\|,</math> which implies that A itself has an inverse.) We may then state that
:::<math>\|(\lambda I-A)^{-1}z\|\leq\frac{1}{\lambda}\|z\|</math>
::for all ''z'' in the range of ''λI'' − ''A''. This is the same inequality as that given at the beginning of this article, with <math>z=(\lambda I-A)x.</math> (We could equally well write these as <math>\|(I-\kappa A)^{-1}z\|\leq\|z\|\text{ or }\|(I-\kappa A)x\|\geq\|x\|</math> which must hold for any positive κ.)

* ''λI'' − ''A'' is [[surjective]] for some ''λ'' > 0 if and only if it is surjective for all ''λ'' > 0. (This is the aforementioned maximally dissipative case.) In that case one has (0, &infin;) &sub; ''ρ''(''A'') (the [[resolvent set]] of ''A'').
* ''A'' is a [[closed operator]] if and only if the range of ''λI'' - ''A'' is closed for some (equivalently: for all) ''λ'' > 0.

==Equivalent characterizations==
Define the duality set of ''x'' ∈ ''X'', a subset of the [[dual space]] ''X''' of ''X'', by

:<math>J(x):=\left\{x'\in X':\|x'\|_{X'}^2=\|x\|_{X}^2=\langle x',x\rangle \right\}.</math>

By the [[Hahn–Banach theorem]] this set is nonempty.<ref>The theorem implies that for a given ''x'' there exists a continuous linear functional φ with the property that φ(''x'')=‖''x''‖, with the norm of φ equal to 1. We identify ‖''x''‖φ with ''x'.''</ref>  In the [[Hilbert space]] case (using the [[Riesz representation theorem|canonical duality]] between a Hilbert space and its dual) it consists of the single element ''x''.<ref>Engel and Nagel Exercise II.3.25i</ref> More generally, if ''X'' is a Banach space with a strictly convex dual, then ''J''(''x'') consists of a single element.<ref>Engel and Nagel Example II.3.26</ref>
Using this notation, ''A'' is dissipative if and only if<ref>Engel and Nagel Proposition II.3.23</ref> for all ''x'' ∈ ''D''(''A'') there exists a ''x''<nowiki>'</nowiki> ∈ ''J''(''x'') such that

:<math>{\rm Re}\langle Ax,x'\rangle\leq0.</math>

In the case of Hilbert spaces, this becomes <math>{\rm Re}\langle Ax,x\rangle\leq0</math> for all ''x'' in ''D''(''A''). Since this is non-positive, we have

:<math>\|x-Ax\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|Ax\|^2-2{\rm Re}\langle Ax,x\rangle\geq\|x\|^2+\|Ax\|^2+2{\rm Re}\langle Ax,x\rangle=\|x+Ax\|^2</math>

:<math>\therefore\|x-Ax\|\geq\|x+Ax\|</math>

Since ''I−A'' has an inverse, this implies that <math>(I+A)(I-A)^{-1}</math> is a [[Contraction (operator theory)|contraction]], and more generally, <math>(\lambda I+A)(\lambda I-A)^{-1}</math> is a contraction for any positive λ. The utility of this formulation is that if this operator is a contraction for '''some''' positive λ then ''A'' is dissipative. It is not necessary to show that it is a contraction for all positive λ (though this is true), in contrast to (λI−A)<sup>−1</sup> which must be proved to be a contraction for '''all''' positive values of λ.

==Examples==

* For a simple finite-dimensional example, consider ''n''-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> with its usual [[dot product]]. If ''A'' denotes the negative of the [[identity operator]], defined on all of '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>, then

::<math>x \cdot A x = x \cdot (-x) = - \| x \|^{2} \leq 0,</math>

: so ''A'' is a dissipative operator.

* So long as the domain of an operator ''A'' (a matrix) is the whole Euclidean space, then it is dissipative if and only if ''A''+''A''<sup>*</sup> (the sum of A and its [[adjoint matrix|adjoint]]) does not have any positive eigenvalue, and (consequently) all such operators are maximally dissipative. This criterion follows from the fact that the real part of <math>x^{*}Ax,</math> which must be nonpositive for any ''x'', is <math>x^{*}\frac{A+A^{*}}2x.</math> The eigenvalues of this [[quadratic form]] must therefore be nonpositive. (The fact that the real part of <math>x^{*}Ax,</math> must be nonpositive implies that the real parts of the eigenvalues of ''A'' must be nonpositive, but this is not sufficient. For example, if <math>A=\begin{pmatrix}-1 & 3 \\0 & -1\end{pmatrix}</math> then its eigenvalues are negative, but the eigenvalues of ''A''+''A''<sup>*</sup> are −5 and 1, so ''A'' is not dissipative.) An equivalent condition is that for some (and hence any) positive <math>\lambda, \lambda-A</math> has an inverse and the operator <math>(\lambda+A)(\lambda-A)^{-1}</math> is a contraction (that is, it either diminishes or leaves unchanged the norm of its operand). If the time derivative of a point ''x'' in the space is given by ''Ax'', then the time evolution is governed by a [[contraction semigroup]] that constantly decreases the norm (or at least doesn't allow it to increase). (Note however that if the domain of ''A'' is a proper subspace, then ''A'' cannot be maximally dissipative because the range will not have a high enough dimensionality.)
* Consider ''H'' = [[Square-integrable function|''L''<sup>2</sup>]]([0, 1]; '''R''') with its usual inner product, and let ''Au'' = ''u''&prime; (in this case a [[weak derivative]]) with domain ''D''(''A'') equal to those functions ''u'' in the [[Sobolev space]] <math>H^1([0,\;1];\;\mathbf{R})</math> with ''u''(1) = 0. ''D''(''A'') is dense in ''L''<sup>2</sup>([0, 1]; '''R'''). Moreover, for every ''u'' in ''D''(''A''), using [[integration by parts]],

::<math>\langle u, A u \rangle = \int_{0}^{1} u(x) u'(x) \, \mathrm{d} x = - \frac1{2} u(0)^{2} \leq 0.</math>

: Hence, ''A'' is a dissipative operator. Furthermore, since there is a solution ([[almost everywhere]]) in ''D'' to <math>u-\lambda u'=f</math> for any ''f'' in ''H'', the operator ''A'' is maximally dissipative. Note that in a case of infinite dimensionality like this, the range can be the whole Banach space even though the domain is only a proper subspace thereof.

* Consider ''H'' = ''H''<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>(Ω; '''R''') (see [[Sobolev space]]) for an [[open set|open]] and [[connected space|connected]] domain Ω &sube; '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> and let ''A'' = Δ, the [[Laplace operator]], defined on the dense subspace of [[compactly supported]] smooth functions on Ω. Then, using integration by parts,

::<math>\langle u, \Delta u \rangle = \int_\Omega u(x) \Delta u(x) \, \mathrm{d} x = - \int_\Omega \big| \nabla u(x) \big|^{2} \, \mathrm{d} x = - \| \nabla u \|^2_{L^{2} (\Omega; \mathbf{R})} \leq 0,</math>

: so the Laplacian is a dissipative operator.<!--I'm commenting this out because I'm not sure exactly what H sub 0 is: However in this case it is not maximally dissipative because there is no compactly supported solution to <math>u-\lambda \Delta u=f</math> if ''f'' is not compactly supported.-->
